title: California serial ‘butt sniffer’ gets slap-on-the-wrist after latest spree went viral on TikTok
text:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.

See more of our coverage in your search results.

A California “butt-sniffer” with more than 40 arrests is headed back to the streets after receiving just 170 days in jail for his latest parole violation, despite a history of targeting women and repeatedly cycling through custody.

Calese Crowder, 39, was arrested Aug. 28 after Glendale police received reports of a man acting suspiciously and allegedly getting close to customers to smell them at multiple businesses.

He was sentenced Tuesday to 170 days in Los Angeles County jail, with 12 days served, and is expected to return to parole once released.

The revolving-door punishment has residents and tough-on-crime critics furious, with critics arguing that California’s soft-on-crime policies have repeatedly failed to keep a habitual offender away from the public.

Around 3:30 p.m. Aug. 28, officers responded to a store in the 1500 block of West Glenoaks Boulevard after reports of a man seen “hunkered down” and getting close to people to smell them, according to the Glendale Police Department.

Officers were also dispatched to a Marshalls near South Brand Boulevard and East Broadway following a similar report.

Crowder was eventually located in the 100 block of South Brand Boulevard and arrested on suspicion of violating his parole.

He was also ordered to stay away from Marshalls, Home Goods and Big Save in Glendale.

Critics say the sentence is merely the latest turn of a revolving door that has done little to stop the alleged behavior.

Crowder served 99 days in late 2025, 105 days in 2026 and now 170 days.

Crowder, a registered sex offender, has a history of similar alleged offenses in Glendale and Burbank dating back to 2021.

He was arrested twice in two months last summer and admitted violating his parole last year, when he was sentenced to more than 100 days in jail.

In 2023, he was arrested for allegedly peeping into a family’s Glendale home.

That August, a woman posted a TikTok video that went viral, allegedly showing Crowder crouching behind her and attempting to sniff her at a Barnes and Noble bookstore in Burbank.

His more than 40 arrests include burglary, robbery, and indecent exposure, and critics say the record demonstrates that California’s lax approach to crime is not doing enough to keep habitual offenders behind bars.

They blame measures including Proposition 47 and Proposition 57, arguing that the laws downgraded many nonviolent property and drug crimes from felonies to misdemeanors and made early release easier.

Parole rules are another flashpoint.

Jail time for a specific parole violation is legally capped, often at 180 days per violation.

Critics argue that a registered sex offender who repeatedly violates conditions intended to keep him away from women should face far more serious consequences.

Some residents fear the behavior could eventually escalate into physical or violent sexual assaults if Crowder is not kept off the streets.

“He needs to be put away for good,” wrote Candice Horry, the wife of former Los Angeles Lakers star Robert Horry, in a social media post.
